title: I had a computer test 1,000 strategies on pure random noise. The best one made +54%.
author: LuckOrEdge
selftext:
AI is very good and a very useful tool for backtesting and finding patterns. The problem is that it finds them even when nothing is there.

If not used properly, AI will give you false results based on assumptions and biases. For example, I made 10 years of fake prices where every move is random, so there is no pattern to find. Then I tested 1,000 simple moving-average strategies on it, a classic case of over optimization.

* 251 of them made money.
* The best one made +54%.

That “best” strategy looks like an edge, but it’s just the luckiest of 1,000 tries.

Then I ran it on 5 more years of random prices it had never seen and itt made −1%.

This is why AI makes the problem worse. It can test thousands of ideas in minutes and show you only the winner. Test enough ideas and one will always look good by luck. This is the classic case of overfitting. 

Two things help:

1. Train your AI model to work around and recognize these biases.
2. Always test your strategy on an out of sample data period. 

AI models are extremely useful tools, but they need to be trained properly in order to get good results.

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
great demo, this is the single most useful experiment anyone can run before trusting a backtest.

one thing puzzled me though: on pure random prices with no fees and no drift, I'd expect roughly half of the 1,000 strategies to end positive, not 251. if only a quarter made money, something in the simulation is pulling everything down, like a negative drift in the generated prices or returns measured in a way that isn't symmetric. worth checking, because it changes what the "+54%" is being compared against.

on the fixes, I'd swap #1 for something more mechanical than training the AI: write down how many strategies were tried and judge the winner against the best of that many random ones. best of 1,000 noise strategies typically shows a t-stat around 3.7, so a winner has to clear that, not zero. and #2 only works if the out-of-sample period gets looked at once. the moment you tweak after seeing it, it quietly becomes in-sample too.

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: Completely agree with you. If you start tweaking your strategy so that it looks good in the out of sample period, you're just overfitting your model.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body: The 20 best going from +40% to -15% is the part that hurts to look at. I had a stretch of optimizing one idea in a lot of different ways and it fell apart on the next period pretty much like that. Now a result that only shows up after a long search makes me more suspicious, not less.

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: I know exactly what you mean. Sometimes you spend weeks/months of working on a strategy only to fail big time in the out of sample period. It's disapointing, but it's part of the work.

comments.author: LuckOrEdge
comments.body: Have you read the post? The post is 100% written by myself other than the image.

comments.author: No-Presentation9797
comments.body:
Welcome to the world of overfitting. :)   

Here's what you can do, take the 5 top strategies, apply them in a fake portfolio, revisit 5 years later and you'll notice that the market is beating you. Sorry to say this, but the markets are efficients. Your AI is finding past overfitted strategies that do not apply to the future...

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: Edges decay over time, but if your edge is strong enough it'll take time. That is why a winning portfolio is one that is not static. It's one where you constantly find new edges and replace them by the ones who have decayed.

replies.author: No-Presentation9797
replies.body: yeah... unfortunately finding 1,000 patterns and choosing the best is easier part. Determining whether the best pattern has real genuine predictive power is the hard part. That's where the overwhelming majority of AI trading experiments are failing and why the majority end up underperforming the overall markets (or exposing the investor to a much higher risk than expected return)
